newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Minister says Russia should go for economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Minister says Russia should go for economic growth.

text.p: Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin on Tuesday signalled concern about Russia's economic course and called for urgent efforts to boost output and forge conditions for growth.

In a letter addressed to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and published in the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily newspaper, he said neither the 1997 budget nor the government's medium-term growth forecasts were realistic.

"If the existing trends in the economy are continued without energetic and purposeful efforts to break them and create real conditions for economic growth, the situation will in all probability continue to get worse," Yasin wrote.
He added: "Growth is...totally imperative for survival and for economic and political stability."
The newspaper, dubbing its report an exclusive, said it was aware that publication of the confidential document could raise hackles in the government.
But it added: "At the end of the day we are talking not about the secret life of one member of the government but about the fate of the whole country."
Russia's current economic policies, based to a large extent on the recipes of the International Monetary Fund, have brought annual inflation to the lowest levels since reforms began.
But output shows few signs of recovering from stubbornly low levels and high interest rates mean companies have little chance of borrowing to invest.

Millions of Russians are living below the poverty line and the opposition dominated State Duma lower house of parliament, which has so far rejected the government's 1997 spending plans, wants ministers to do more to protect the poor.
But Yasin said revenue forecasts should be scaled down and both social and defence spending had to be cut, even if this increased the risk of political unrest.

"The coming two years will be more favourable for reforms and for a policy of reviving growth," he said. "A realistic programme of action which can convince people of the chance of success without populism has more chance of being trusted."
The minister said the government's latest three-year plan, which predicts annual growth of five percent by the year 2000, did not properly examine the real risks facing the Russian economy.
He said lower interest rates -- a key government aim -- would not by itself be enough to stimulate growth quickly.
"We cannot count on this," he said. "It could take too long, during which time the degradation of the economy will continue, possibly with irreversible consequences."
Yasin, apparently criticising Chernomyrdin, said old policies of "concessions and indulgencies" to lobby groups were dragging Russia into an abyss.
"The policy of balancing different interests groups...was to some extent justified in the period before the (presidential) elections," he said.
"But it has outlived its usefulness and its continuation is dragging the country into the abyss of a long depression which is increasing the threat of new political shocks."
Many outside analysts say vested interests -- banks and monopolist producers such as energy giant Gazprom -- have an undue influence on Russian economic policy.
Gazprom, once Chernomyrdin's fiefdom, faces criticism for tax arrears, although the company, the world's biggest producer of natural gas, says it is owed much more money than it owes.
Other companies have big tax arrears as well and the IMF has postponed payments on a three-year $10 billion loan because it is worried about low tax revenues.
